**Commentary of al-Biqaʿi (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):**

Sūrat Nūn, also called Sūrat al-Qalam (the Chapter of the Pen).

Its central purpose is to make manifest what was hidden, and to clarify what was left vague in the verse ﴿So you will know who is in clear error﴾. This is done by specifying the one who is guided, whose guidance is demonstrated by his possession of knowledge, which is the greatest light. Through companionship with it one does not go astray, by receiving the Qur'an and by taking on the character of the Criterion (al-Furqan), which is an attribute of the Most Merciful, to the extent of human capacity, as far as human power can reach. The most indicative things in the surah for this purpose are the letter ﴿Nūn﴾ and likewise the ﴿Pen﴾. For this reason the surah is named after each of them, and by discussing each one this becomes known. The summary of this is that the letter nūn is a clarifier that encompasses in its clarifying, just as the light of the sun encompasses what it makes visible (p-273), and just as the inkwell encompasses its ink, with the sign of what it indicates through its point of articulation and its attributes. The discourse that falls within it is settled, and so are the meanings that share its form. It causes the pen to die out, since its making knowledge clear is a matter that cannot be denied. ﴿In the name of God﴾, to whom belongs complete encompassment, so He is over all things powerful, because He is with all things knowing. ﴿The Most Gracious﴾, whose blessing of bringing into existence has embraced the people of the Return, both the sound and the sick among them. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, who completes that blessing for whomever He grants success in obeying Him, so He makes him keep to the straight path.

* *

When He left vague the one who is astray and the one who is guided at the end of Sūrat al-Mulk, and the wrongdoer and the good-doer in their deeds at its beginning, and concluded with the verse of the flowing water, whose letters together indicate the completeness of its meaning, and each of which indicates something of it: its mīm indicates a complete, manifest thing; its ʿayn indicates a guiding sign; its yāʾ indicates a gentle, standing presence that descends with every station; and its nūn indicates a manifest clarifier that encompasses what it manifests. He, glorified be He, returned them to it after their straying from it, by the interrogation in this verse, with what He alerted them to regarding their own incapacity and the incapacity of everyone they call upon besides Him. And that He is not able to bring that water, which is the life of forms after its disappearance, except one whose power is complete. Thus He was able over everything He wills. And He was not able to bring about [everything - ] what He wills except one whose knowledge is perfect, by which He revives the dead of spirits. He indicated the comprehensiveness of His power through the completeness of His knowledge, by what He bestowed upon the noble, unlettered Prophet of the sciences whose seas overflowed, so that He revived their channels (p-274) and drowned their currents. So He opened this surah with the word of clarification, which is the name of the letter that is the last of those letters. It is one of the necessary consequences of some of what the water indicates, which is the sound life. He drew attention to His having appointed it as a sign of the knowledge of what it indicates: of its point of articulation, its names, its attributes, and its positions in words, in all its transformations. So He said: ﴿Nūn﴾. This word is a letter of the alphabet, and it is a name for something by which the manifestation of things, their knowledge, and their perception occur, as indicated by its position in the words for light, fire, the Nile, growth, distinction, purity, advice, news, nobility, salvation, carving, and regret. It has already been mentioned in al-Baqara that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is these letters," and none knows what they are except the One who set them, glorified be He.

Since this letter is shared in the language between the letter of the alphabet, the inkwell, the fish, and the blade of a sword, it rested, at the outset, on indicating that it is a letter. Its inherent quiescence in its form does not prevent the intent of the remaining meanings, because the Arabs sometimes pause on a word with the intention of stopping, to draw attention to the greatness of its meaning. So the quiescence does not imply anything beyond the absence of the vowel-forming factor. It is said: the nūn is the tablet, the nūna is a word of truth, and the fish. So it is suitable for the universal letter of the alphabet, which is suitable for [every - ] individual. And from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that he gave precedence to the letters of [al-Rahman - ], and to the inkwell, because of the knowledge that flows from it, and to the fish upon whose back the cosmos rests, whose name is Yahmut, because of the wonders of destiny and secrets in that. The oath was sworn by the nūn and the pen, as an elevation for encompassment. And by the sword, because of the great effects that flow from it. Whatever the intended meaning, it is encompassment, and it is an inner secret that does not appear, but whose results appear. So it is the judgment, and its results are the decree and destiny, either to misery or to happiness.

Since this letter is the sign of the disclosure of things, its point of articulation is among the most accessible, the easiest, the lightest, and the most widespread of points of articulation. It is the head of what is spoken, for it emerges from between the tip of the tongue and the area above the upper incisors on the gum. It is further forward than the point of articulation of the lām and also than that of the rāʾ. These three letters, together with the rest of the letters of the phrase fārra min lubb, are called the slippery letters (al-zalaqiyya, letters articulated at the tip of the tongue), because the tip of anything is slippery. The nūn is the most fitting of them in this point of articulation, and the firmest in closure between the tongue and the gum. It is among those whose name repeats its referent in its own name, so it ends where it began. It is distinguished by the fact that its pillar and foundation is the strongest, most manifest letter, the one of elevation and height, which is the wāw. The slippery letter of which it is one is the opposite of the solid letters (al-musmata, letters articulated more firmly and stably). The slippery letters are the lightest on the tongue and the most intermixed with others. As for the solid letters, they are prevented from standing alone in the language of the Arabs in a word of more than three letters. Rather, some of the slippery letters must accompany them. The alif lies outside both categories, for it is merely airs with no fixed place. Its point of articulation is suited to its breadth and lightness. It is described as slippery, and the perfection that comes to those characterized by these letters is sufficient for it without anything else. Nothing that is not mixed with perfection in these respects can attain what has been mentioned, that its meaning is clarification and manifestation. Among its attributes are voicing, and being between hardness and softness, openness, and lowering. And the nasal resonance coming out of the nasal passage when it is quiescent. All of this is clear in the knowledge that has breadth, spread, and penetration into hidden things. The mīm shares with it the nasal resonance, just as it [shares with it that it has a share of manifestness, and the nūn is the origin of the nasal resonance, just as it is - ] the origin of manifestness, because of its elevation by its pillar. It is also one of the letters of fluctuation and addition, which never settle in one state, so that they sometimes occur as additions and sometimes as roots. Just as knowledge too has no stability: however much you broaden it, it broadens, and however much you leave it, it vanishes and contracts. It is also one of the interchangeable letters (al-ibdal), which are replaced by others, and cannot be replaced by others as their substitute, except in necessity. The mīm's necessary replacement of the bāʾ is an exception, not the reverse. Just as knowledge is a root that others follow, and it does not itself follow others. It is one of the sound letters and not weak ones. Knowledge is worthy of this description. And when it is hidden, it is of the letters that are mixed (al-mushraba, letters with a breathy, blended quality), which are called (p-277) the mixed letters (al-mukhalaṭa), with kasra and fatḥa on the lām. These are the letters the Arabs expanded upon, adding them to the twenty-nine in use, and they are among the hard letters (al-ṣumm), which are all except the throat letters. They were so named because of their firm placement in exiting the mouth and their stability within it. It is said of something firm and solid: al-muṣtamm. Knowledge is most suited to this description. Since it has matched in its point of articulation and all its attributes with knowledge, which is the purpose of the surah, it has clearly become evident that it is its purpose.

As for the rank of the pen in clarifying knowledge, manifesting it, unveiling its hidden matters and secrets, and spreading and publicizing it, it is of a degree that no one endowed with intellect fails to know. Among the things distinctive to this letter is that it accompanies every letter. Its limit is what the tanwīn expresses, whose arrangement with the vowels is what its sign, the perfecting knowledge, is. ﴿By it life﴾ is the sign of what these vowels express. Since these vowels are a sign of what life is, the tanwīn after them is a sign of what the perfection of life consists in, namely knowledge. It is the cause of what standing and manifestation depend on. And among its meanings is the name of God, the Light. Then it is a name for everything that makes manifest what was hidden inwardly, like knowledge in perception, by which the realities of things appear. And outwardly, like the two luminaries for the eyes, and all other lights, outward and inward. And what is a means of manifestation, like the eyes, by which things are seen and their forms appear (p-278). And the inkwell from which is the ink of what is written with the pen in the worlds, highest and lowest, and every instrument by which one reaches the manifestation of a form. It is perfectly like the water of the cloud, which is the ink of everything God created the beings and the beginnings with. ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾. From it also comes the meaning of the plant star, which for the tree is like the fava bean for the human, clothed in light (nūr, with a fatḥa), which has a share of light (nūr, with a ḍamma). And the dhurʾ, which is manifest in itself and a manifestation of the paths of guidance. Likewise the matter with fire that is purified from the rank of its darkness, which is its ultimate, and its beginning is what comes out of it: wood, iron, and stone.

Since this letter is the name of what makes a matter manifest, it is not restricted to any one of the manifesting things to the exclusion of another. Rather it includes light, the sense organ, the will, and the matter. For this reason it came with the kāf, which is the knowledge of creation, as the cause of the manifestation of everything: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40]. And because of its applicability to [every - ] manifestation, Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, explained it as the inkwell, so he explained it by that from which the pen draws its ink. Let attention be paid to its position in najd, for it is the name for what rises up from the earth, and appears in itself, and makes other things appear. And in nuhūd (the swelling of breasts) of a young girl, which is the manifestation of her breast. And in nahb (plunder), which is what is taken openly, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let him not plunder a plunder of honor, to which people raise their eyes." And in nafkh (blowing), nafʿ (benefit), naṣr (victory), naqr (tapping), naqb (piercing), and what resembles them, for all of these are manifestation (p-279) and making manifest, like nammu, manna, and namaʾ. And because of its height and its inward character, and because it is the complete encompassment of the manifesting clarifier, its standing is elevated above the alif, which is the wāw, and it ends at what it began with. And because the mīm is complete, its standing rests on a descending thing, like the alif, which is the yāʾ in your saying mīm. And because the wāw returns to the height of the alif, its pillar is the alif in your saying wāw. These three letters are manifest in two worlds: the one they begin with is outward, and the one they end with is inward. The first nūn expresses the light of the eyes, and the final one expresses the light of the heart. And since the hāʾ is the odd of the dāl, and it is encompassing, inward, hidden, it was necessary that the place of its doubling by the yāʾ be an encompassing, inward place, of low rank in the unseen relative to the hāʾ, because it falls in the ranks of tens, and that is the nūn. So it was manifest relative to the hiddenness of the hāʾ, and inward relative to the manifestness of the mīm. Thus by the nūn is the manifestation of the mīm, which expresses "the Dominion" (al-mulk) that preceded in the previous surah, just as the witnessing of the dāl and its firmness is by the hāʾ.

Therefore the completion of every work is founded on a light of knowledge, just as the upholding of the apparent aspect of every letter (other than the hāʾ) depends on it. The nūn served as ink for knowledge like this, which displays their forms through the line of the pen. The sign of what is hidden in it, which the pen made manifest, is the nūn beneath the earth, upon which the earth rests (p. 280). It is the first thing the people of Paradise eat: the liver-lobe of the ox upon which the earth rests, which is slaughtered for them, as reported in the tradition. The hidden nūn in the earth is matched by the qāf manifest on its surface, which is the mountain of emerald surrounding the world. Dominion over hearts in this world is achieved only through knowledge, which is the reality of the nūn, just as dominion over bodies in the outward world is achieved only through power, which is the reality of the qāf. This is as appears from the circulation of the scholars in the hidden nūn and the kings in the manifest qāf. These two categories of creation are the ones who hold sway over people through governance and the enforcement of command. For this reason the detailed portion of the Qur'an (al-mufaṣṣal, the later short surahs) was established upon the two letters qāf and nūn. These two letters are also combined in the word "Qur'an" and in the word "Furqān," which are among its outward names. The first thing the people of Paradise eat is from the ox upon which the world rests, which used to graze at the edges of Paradise, as reported from him, upon whom be the most excellent prayers and peace. This is because the image of the ox is the meaning of toil, exertion and the strenuous labour upon the earth on which the affairs of the world are established. When the people of this world are first relieved of the matter of the world by bringing forward the matter of toil before their livelihood in Paradise, the one slaughtered for them is the ox, which is the image of their toil, and they eat it. It is the recompense for what they did in their worldly life, insofar as they were people of religion (p. 281). Thus they deserved the recompense of their toil by means of what is its image. Added to this is the liver-lobe of the nūn, which is the image of their share of the root of knowledge. They ate it and were rewarded with it. Account was taken in their deeds of the goodness of their intention in the foundation of their religion. When they reached these two, they encountered rest and freedom from hardship in their livelihood in Paradise. What drew them by Him, glory be to Him, to the years of this rank is what He perfected in His wisdom from the praise of the detailed Qur'anic portion for the two letters qāf, through which there is strength, subjugation and power, and nūn, through which this is made manifest to the intellect by the light of knowledge.

This is because the Qur'an, which He, glory be to Him, sent down as mathānī (oft-repeated), included in what lies beyond the detailed portion, from qāf to the end of the Noble Book, and in its opening, what pertains to the people of knowledge and understanding: expanded rulings, decisive legal injunctions, lengthy narratives and ambiguous verses. It also includes the surahs opening with the disjointed letters, whose supreme comprehensiveness is unseen and whose direction rests upon units of numbers. Of these, the knowledge of the outward meaning belongs specifically to the community (al-ummah), and the matter of their inward meaning belongs to the Family of Muhammad (ﷺ). Because of the high rank of the presentation of what lies beyond the detailed portion, the Real, exalted be He, doubled the address and arranged it in surahs that are many in number and small in verse-count, which is the detailed portion. In these He mentioned, from the edges of narratives, admonitions, rulings, reports and the matter of recompense, what suits the hearing of the common people, so that it would be easy for them to hear and so that they would take (p. 282) a portion of what the elite took. It is repeated in their ears through the recitation of the imams in the obligatory prayers, from which there is no escape for them, so that it becomes familiar to them, of what would otherwise escape them from the content of the other long surahs. Therefore the most fitting way to open their detailed portion was with the letter qāf, which is the odd unit (waṭr al-āḥād), until it became ten. Then, when it is multiplied by itself, it becomes one hundred. The detailed portion was therefore opened with it, so that the content it contains would be more manifest than the content of what opens with alif-lām-mīm. For this reason he (ﷺ) would frequently recite in the Friday sermon the surah "Qāf," opening for the common people, to whom the Friday sermon is addressed, since it is a comprehensive prayer in its outward form, with the opening of the specific detailed portion. Its content includes, from the meaning of power and subjugation, what is needed for upholding the affairs of the common people, which is sufficient. It is paired with the surah "Nūn," which manifests the outward aspect of "Qāf." Thus they are specified with what contains subjugation and clarity. The surah "Nūn" is specific, from the requirement of knowledge, with what encompasses the affairs of the common people, which ends at the goal of the Remembrance that comprehends all worlds. This is because the power that expresses knowledge may sometimes have harm greater than its benefit, as one of the early generations (salaf) said: "Every honour not established by knowledge ends in humiliation." Just as all the twenty-nine surahs opening with the letters, which include the nine ranks in the nine units and the tenth which gathers the nine ranks through the odd numbers of its units, and the tenth that gathers multiplies the tenfold odd in itself, establishing (qiwām) and encompassing (p. 283) [in all of the Qur'an, so likewise the surah "Qāf" and the surah "Nūn" are a specific establishment and specific encompassing] specifically of what belongs to the common people of the Qur'an, which the earth gathers, by what encompasses its outward aspect from the form of the mountain of "Qāf," and what encompasses its inward aspect from the form of the creature of "Nūn." The completion of their affair lies between the two supports that establish them. Through this surah that opens with the letters, the distinctiveness of the Qur'an appeared, and it was distinguished from the rest of the books, because it includes a comprehensiveness that is found only in the Seal, the all-gathering. In its surahs, the detail that suits its comprehensiveness is combined. Because of the comprehensiveness of its meanings and their ambiguity, whatever meaning the exegete (mufassir) explains from them that returns to their requirement is sound in its encompassing of what descends from them of the Names of God and their arrangement in all worlds. Therefore no exegete errs in them, because whenever he intends an aspect of the interpretation, he does not go outside the comprehensiveness of what it requires. And whatever they are interpreted as: from the Names of God, or from the names of angels, or from the names of prophets, or from [similar] things, or from images of existents, or that they are oaths God swore by, or openings by which surahs are identified, or numbers indicating events and portions of outward or inward matters according to differing ranks and conditions, of what was given to the one upon whom it was sent down (ﷺ), (p. 284) such as the measure of the term of the caliphate, kingdom and sovereignty, what his affair ends with of the manifestation of guidance, and similar things, encompassing the term of his day and beyond that. Each of these falls within their comprehensiveness. For this reason also they are not restricted to a specific position that requires a specific sign of inflection. Whatever is assigned to their positions in this surah, whether genitive, nominative or accusative, falls within the comprehensiveness of their rank, and no specific meaning is required of them, because they have no fixed connection. They are self-sufficient and encompassing, and the connection arises only where the meaning of each of the connected elements is completed by the attainment of the connection. This applies, among words, only to those that fall short of the comprehensiveness of the content of the letters. So whenever self-sufficiency and comprehensiveness occur in a word, no connection occurs in it.

Since the establishment of this existence is by the sword and the pen, and since "nūn" is shared among meanings, of which are the sword, the inkwell which is the instrument of the pen, and the tablet which is the locus of what is established of knowledge, and since the sword had already been placed in the domain of the qāf with which the surah "Qāf" opens, as this is most appropriate, since it includes strength, power and subjugation in the surah of Iron (al-Ḥadīd), after the exhortation, the threat and the reminder of blessings in the surah that falls between them (p. 285), He mentioned here what belongs to the domain of the nūn of the sign of knowledge, saying after the letter "nūn," swearing: ﴿By the pen﴾, that is, the pen of power, which is the first thing God originated. Then He said to it: "Write." It inscribed all creatures until the Day of Resurrection in the Preserved Tablet in reality, and in the tablets of the pages of creatures in state and in metaphor. Thus it manifested all sciences. Then He sealed its mouth, so it did not speak and does not speak until the Day of Resurrection. What creation writes is what God bestowed upon them of those knowledges and understandings, and that is the establishment of the affairs of the world. The indication by it is to the decree, which is among the results of "nūn," because it is among God's manifest creations, whose wisdom, glory be to Him, required its existence, and He directed it to detail what the judgement had decided.

Since what is achieved by the pen of spreading reports and spreading sciences in their diversity and secrets exceeds counting, it became as if it were the all-knowing world and the eloquent speaker of logic. Its meaning being the genus, He attributed to it what is attributed to rational beings, so He said: ﴿and what they inscribe﴾, that is, the pen of power. He made its plural take the course of those possessing knowledge, for exalting it, because it performs their actions. Or "the pens" is meant as a genus. It is also possible that the attribution is to those who write with it, since what is indicated by it of them is mentioned. As for the angels, if what is meant is what they wrote in the Clear Book and the Preserved Tablet and elsewhere of what they write (p. 286), and as for every one of them and of others who writes, even the people of the unjust document in which they conspired to boycott the Banū Hāshim and those who abandoned them until they would hand over to them the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to do with him as they pleased, however that may be, it is an indication of what was decreed, because it is only what He has decreed and judged that is inscribed.

(p-287) Since the one addressed here, ﷺ, had lived among the people to whom he was sent for a long span of time, forty years, and he was the most exalted of them in rank, the purest of them in character, the most firm of them in intellect, the most sound of them in judgment, the most compassionate of them, and the most elevated of them in aspiration above the taints of baseness, and the purest of them in soul, to the extent that among them he was called by no name but "the Trustworthy" (al-Amin), and nothing had newly appeared in him that would warrant their describing him with madness, the madness that produces error from the aims mentioned at the end of the surah in His saying: ﴿So you will know who is in clear error﴾ [al-Mulk: 29], except the blessing which no one had ever received, in any age of the ages or any era of the eras, he responded to this great oath, rejecting their claim in the clearest and most evident manner, to make him at ease, and to ease his heart and calm his inner self, from the loneliness that their slander had caused him: ﴿You are not﴾, that is, O most worthy of those addressed by Our speech, ﴿by the blessing﴾, that is, by the bounty of ﴿your Lord﴾, who has nurtured you with such lofty aspirations and perfect qualities, by singling you out with the Qur'an, which comprises every knowledge and wisdom. He emphasised the negation to increase his honour, ﷺ, and said: ﴿mad﴾. That is, [rather] the one who described you with this is the one truly deserving the name of madness. Its meaning, apart from the error which he repeated at the end of that, between you and them about it, is that of following the path of fairness, so that they might consider it through the evidence, and thus know their own error and your guidance, through the decisive proof of reflecting on the signs that make this manifest in the fullest manifestation. Thus He negated from him ﷺ the wretchedness that is caused by corruption of the intellect, and the happiness caused by soundness of the intellect and the Lord's blessing upon him was thereby established.

[And] the Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since Surat al-Mulk contains such great proofs that the intellects cannot exhaust the reflection upon even some of them, such as the reflection upon the creation of the heavens in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who created seven heavens in layers﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, some of them correspond to one another (yuṭābiqu). From ṭābaqa al-na'l (he matched the sandal), meaning when he stitched it, layer upon layer (ṭabaqan 'ala ṭabaq). This suggests their equality in the extent of their regions and the measures of their bodies, and Allah knows best. The description by the verbal noun (maṣdar) suggests a firm correspondence of some of them to others, as an announcement from Him, glorified and exalted is He, that despite their great bodies and the distances of their regions, some of them correspond to others without excess or deficiency: ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, no disparity, disorder or contradiction in the creation. Rather, it is uniform and straight. The apparent noun was used in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], and He did not say "You see no discrepancy in it," to indicate that all created things proceed according to this, each form suited to its form, with no discrepancy in any of that and no disorder. Thus the apparent noun gave a generality that the pronoun would not have given. As the specific name al-Rahman also suggested, through these extended proofs, the mercy to creatures for whoever is granted reflection. Then He, exalted is He, drew attention to what removes doubt and dispels the difficulty in this, and said: ﴿Then return the gaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, repeat reflection, and contemplate what you witness of these created things until what you have been told becomes certain to you through direct observation, and no doubt remains with you about it.

﴿Do you see any flaws?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, any fissures or cracks. Then He, exalted is He, commanded repeated gazing at them, scanning and savouring, to see whether you find any defect or flaw: ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], that is, when you do this, your gaze will return far from attaining what it seeks, as if it were driven away with abasement, exhaustion and weariness, because of the length of the repetition and the reiteration. He commanded the return of the gaze so that in this there might be its rest and its readiness, so that it does not, in the first return, fall into heedlessness and distraction, until its gaze becomes exhausted from long repetition, since the meaning of the dual in His saying "twice" (karratayn) is repetition, like their saying labbayka wa-sa'dayka (at Your service, again and again). So the gaze becomes exhausted from long repetition and does not stumble upon any fissure. Had the surah contained nothing other than what has occurred from its beginning to here, there would be in that the greatest lesson and the clearest proof for whoever seeks insight, since this reflection, with the generality mentioned, applies to all created things, and its modes of operation can be grasped only by individuals of the intelligent after stimulation and alerting. So its testimony to the prophethood of the one who brought it is established and clear. Then the signs have been repeated in the surah, such as His saying: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], and His saying: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ [al-Mulk: 14], and the verses to the end of the surah. The least of these is sufficient for reflection. How, then, could one who is described by some of what they mocked him with, in their saying "mad," "sorcerer," "poet," and "liar," produce these?

﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14]. Because of the greatness of the proofs contained in Surat al-Mulk, I followed it, in declaring far removed from what the falsifiers ascribed to him the one who brought it, Muhammad ﷺ, swearing to that for added exaltation, as a confirmation in honouring and repetition. So the Exalted said: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ [al-Qalam: 1], ﴿You are not, by the blessing of your Lord, mad﴾. And how could it be right for someone mad to conceive even some of those proofs, before which the perceptions of the intelligent have been cut off, let alone to set them out and clarify them in a concise order, a miraculous composition, a harmony that dazzles the intellects, and an expression that surpasses every saying, known but not grasped, its paths made clear yet not walked? ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like﴾ [al-Isra': 88]. So His saying, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿You are not, by the blessing of your Lord, mad﴾ is an answer to His saying at the end of the surah, ﴿Indeed, he is mad﴾ [al-Qalam: 51]. The answer came first by negating their claim and declaring him free of it, as a report of their words, so that it would be more eloquent in his honour, ﷺ, and lighter in its impact upon him, and would more comfortably settle his state in receiving it from them. For this reason He put first the praise of him, ﷺ, with what he was singled out for of great character. This was more effective in exalting him than placing their statement first and then refuting it. By breaking the force of that hideous claim with the prior declaration of his freedom from it, the purpose is more complete and perfect. There is no more suitable place for mentioning his freedom from such things, peace and blessings be upon him, and describing him with the character and noble gifts with which he is described, than this, since some of what Surat al-Mulk contains, with what was previously alluded to, is a decisive witness for every intelligent person who acknowledges the soundness of his prophethood, ﷺ, and the sublime nature of his truthfulness.

﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. The position of this surah here has thus become clear, and the harmony of what follows its verses is mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis). End.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on surah 68, verse 3:

When He, glorified is He, negated from him ﷺ what they had said, of the things they had slandered him with, thereby establishing for him ﷺ perfection of intellect, and since the madman is one who has no action that is orderly nor speech that is coherent, so that no one employs him in anything in order that he have a reward for it, He affirmed for him the reward, which necessarily implies intellect. Its affirmation is thus realized from the Most Wise of the wise, in a manner more eloquent than if He had stated it explicitly. So He said, for emphasis, given their denial of it while they claimed about him the falsehood of slander: ﴿And indeed for you﴾, that is, in return for what you have borne of the burdens of prophethood and for your patience with them in the face of what they hurl at you. This is consolation for him ﷺ: ﴿a reward﴾. And since He affirmed for him what accompanies intellect and is suitable both for this world and for the Hereafter, indicated by its indefiniteness (tanwin) and by what the context implies of praising him ﷺ for his greatness, and since a reward does not necessarily imply permanence, and may be spoiled by some kind of obligation, He said: ﴿unending﴾, that is, uninterrupted and not diminished, in your worldly life nor in your Hereafter, nor for anyone among the people (p-292) upon you [ by it - ] an act by which he would impose an obligation, by mentioning it in the manner of reproach and rebuke. This is the explanation of felicity. A reward is only given for righteous action, and action refines character, so it is suited to the outcome of good character and sound intellect.

When this intellect was established, along with the excellence it conferred, and since the one who is rewarded may possess only the lowest degree of intellect, [the verse] showed that he (ﷺ) possessed its highest degree, by His saying, emphasizing what came before: ﴿And indeed you﴾. He increased the emphasis because of their increased obstinacy, so He said: ﴿are upon a great character﴾. Since the context implied magnification, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿great﴾. This [great character] is Islam, to which the Qur'an calls, not a character that turns aside under trials or changes with gifts. This is because his character, as attested by the one who knew him best, his wife Umm al-Mu'minin al-Siddiqah 'Aisha bint al-Siddiq Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, was the Qur'an. He does not move or rest except by His command and prohibition. This character is the result of guidance, and guidance is the result of intellect, and it is the cause of happiness. Thus it indicates that their lack of happiness was due to the lack of their intellects. [And] al-Wasiti said: Allah manifested His power in 'Isa, peace be upon him, His executing will in Asaf, and His wrath and subjugation in the staff of Musa, peace be upon him. And He manifested His character and attributes in Muhammad (ﷺ), so he was characterized by the character of Allah the Exalted. To be characterized by His character is to exalt His knowledge above ignorance, His generosity above stinginess, His justice above injustice, and His forbearance above foolishness. Know that creation (khalq) and character (khuluq) are two forms: khalq is the form of the outward, and khuluq is the form of the inward. The proportion of the outward limbs is expressed by good creation, and the proportion of the inner meanings is expressed by good character. Then good character is sometimes with Allah, sometimes with the judgment of Allah, and sometimes with creation. With Allah, it is through veneration and reverence. With His judgment, it is through patience in hardship and adversity, gratitude in ease, compliance with His commands, and restraint from His prohibitions, done with a willing heart, eagerly and generously. Good character with creation is spreading fairness in dealings and good courtesy in companionship. It was related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said:

"Character is the vessel of religion, for religion comes out of character. It is humility, submissiveness, surrendering oneself to Allah, and bearing what is disliked."

(p-294) Since Islam is the most noble of religions, God Most High bestowed upon it the strongest and most noble of moral qualities, which is *al-ḥayāʾ* (modesty, shame before wrongdoing). It has been related that every religion has a distinctive character, and the distinctive character of Islam is modesty. From modesty comes the life of the heart. Thus he (ﷺ) would accept what is easy from people (*al-ʿafw*), enjoin what is customary (*al-ʿurf*), and turn away from the ignorant. He would not repay an evil deed with an evil deed; rather he would pardon, overlook, and do good in spite of it. Someone would pull on his cloak so hard that it left a mark on his neck, and he would turn around laughing and fulfil the needs of the one who pulled and treat him kindly. Thus the directing decree (*al-kalām al-tadbīrī*), indicated by the letter *nūn*, and the universal effecting decree (*al-qaḍāʾ al-kullī al-taʾthīrī*), indicated by the *qalam* (pen), and the firm detailed destiny (*al-qadar al-mubram al-tafṣīlī*), which falls upon the setting of the decree and is indicated by the *saṭr* (line), are all included in this. An example of this: whoever wants to build a waterwheel first needs an engineer who, by his knowledge, determines the place of the well, the axle, the position of the bucket, the position of the channels, and the like. This is the directing ruling (*al-ḥukm al-tadbīrī*). Second, he needs a workman who digs the well and builds, and a carpenter who assembles the wood according to the engineer's wisdom. This is the effecting decree (*al-qaḍāʾ al-taʾthīrī*). Third, he needs the setting of the wheel in its place, the turning of the bucket-chain with its pots, and the flow of water in the channels according to the decree, and this is the destiny (*al-qadar*). Fourth and fifth, it requires explaining the division of what is decreed into the wretched and the happy. The ruling is hidden, a secret of His secrets, glory be to Him and exalted is He. Glory be to Him, whose measure none knows but Himself.

(p-295) When God, glory be to Him, swore an oath to negate what they had slandered him with, and indicated by both explicit statement and allusion what He had bestowed upon him of perfect intellect and complete nobility and eminence, the matter was established with the utmost certainty through the reports of the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. He then indicated it by direct observation, in a manner that is among the signs of prophethood, to judge the future. So He said, consequently upon the truth of this report: ﴿So you will see﴾, that is, you will know, O most exalted, noblest and most perfect of creation, soon, by a promise that admits no failure, a knowledge in whose certainty you are like one who sees with clear sight. ﴿And they will see﴾, that is, those who accused you of slander will know with a knowledge that is exactly so.

Since he (ﷺ) and those with him formed one party, and the enemies formed another, and the last part of the sentence left the misguided kingdom's (position) ambiguous between the two parties, He said: ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one﴾, i.e., in which of your two parties is ﴿the afflicted one﴾ [i.e.] afflicted with misguidance and madness, to the point of turning away from guidance and the religion of truth. Or (it means): which of you has the affliction (fitnah) of madness and other things, taking it as a verbal noun (masdar) of fitan. Al-Razi said: it is a masdar like al-maftun, and it means madness in the language of the Quraysh, as one says: "He has no ma'qul" and "he has no majlud," meaning intellect and endurance.

Since this was a report of their madness, which entails their going astray in this described manner, and since such a statement may occur in people's discourse as a kind of conjecture, Allah, exalted is He, resumed with what serves as the justification for the judgment that the context had conveyed against them, to inform that it arises from certain knowledge with no doubt whatsoever. So He said, emphasizing it because of their denial that the matter could be as the preceding context indicated: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, that is, the One who nurtured you in the finest nurturing and fashioned you upon the greatest of characters, ﴿He﴾, that is, alone, ﴿is most knowing﴾ [that is, ] of everyone, especially of one who is ﴿of those who have strayed﴾, that is, who has gone astray, erred, deviated, slipped, become lost, and vanished into a great disappearance from which he finds no guidance, took a path other than the straight way, missed the place of right guidance, turning away ﴿from His way﴾. Thus he was the most insane of the insane, because He, glorified and exalted, is their Creator and Lawgiver, "Should He not know whom He created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" [Qur'an 67:14]. This is especially so since He is the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting, who does not neglect. ﴿And He﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿is most knowing of the guided﴾, that is, those who remain firm upon guidance, and they are the people of intellect and sound judgment. This is the secret of destiny, of which it is said that it only becomes manifest on the Day of Reckoning (al-Haqqah).

Since it is part of human nature that the forbearing and steady among them, when harm from one who does not usually behave like their kind grows severe against him, will draw close to them, and he does not accuse those over whom the disagreement arises of being somewhat too close, and the cause of that closeness is only his lack of knowledge of the outcomes, God (subhanahu) mentioned, by way of what preceded from His informing him (p-297) of the realities of affairs and His unveiling of their hidden aspects, His saying as a goading and stirring to steadfastness in their disobedience, and as an informing of the misguided one by its signs so that the guided one may know, for things are known by their opposites. It is an address to him (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, so that this may be more forceful in their hearing: ﴿So do not obey﴾, that is, O you who are commanded to rescue them from the perils of their desires and the snares of their destruction, ﴿the deniers﴾, that is, those deeply immersed in denial. Al-Malawi said: It is not hidden that every disbelief that appeared, every misguidance that appeared, and every innovation and every evil, its cause was only the corruption of the cognitive and articulate faculty, and that occurs through denial.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 9:

Then he gave the reason for that, with that whose totality would be upon its occurrence from them over a long period while they persist in it, by his saying: ﴿They wish﴾, i.e., they love with a great, wide love, exceeding the limit, long ago, with persistence in that. He emphasized their eagerness for this wish with what conveys longing, and that this is persistent from them, not that it occurred and passed. So he said, pointing to their corrupting the faculty of speech and the creation of natural courage: ﴿if you would compromise﴾, i.e., you would be soft and agree to some of (p-298) what they desire, so that you would make a truce with them by leaving off forbidding them from polytheism, leaving off confronting their gods with reviling and their minds with ridicule and their fathers with misguidance. Ibn Burjan said: "Compromise (idhan) is softness, being drawn into falsehood, and turning a blind eye to the truth while knowing it - end."

It is from the word duhn (oil), because it softens what is oiled with it.

Since it was their nature that they would soften toward him ﷺ at certain times [as deception], as was said concerning the occasion of revelation of "al-Kafirun", that they said to him ﷺ: "Come, let us reconcile: we will worship your god for a year and you worship our gods for a year," and similar of the falsehoods, to the point that they prostrated behind him ﷺ when he recited to them Surat al-Najm, and he prostrated in it, so the unbelievers, the believers, the jinn and mankind all prostrated behind him, until the emigrants to Abyssinia heard of it while they were in Abyssinia, so some of them returned [supposing - ] that they had embraced Islam, and found them in the same vile state they had been in at first. He, glorified is He, said, making known that this from them is deception: ﴿so they would compromise﴾, i.e., because of their love, that you would be soft [they - ] would compromise. So it is coordinated with [«they wish» not - ] the answer to «if» for the sake of alerting him ﷺ that their softness is only deception, intended for nothing but corruption. They delayed the compromise, although they had long loved him, hoping that he would begin with it, whereupon they would show it then. Al-Qushayri said: "Whoever wakes up ill wishes that all people were sick."

When He forbade him to obey the one who denies and gave the reason for it, and since some people among them concealed their denial, He said, setting out the marks of the one who denies: ﴿And do not obey﴾, that is, at any time, whether from among them or from others, ﴿every habitual swearer﴾, that is, one who exaggerates in daring to swear oaths, even if his denial has not become apparent to you. The intent is not a prohibition of the general category but the generality of the prohibition. That is, "Refrain from every habitual swearer." The prohibition is the basic principle, and "every" applies to it. The same construction was explained previously at the end of al-Baqarah in His saying, ﴿Allah does not love every disbelieving sinner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276]. These attributes branch out from lying and corrupt disposition, so they are like a detailed explanation. Frequent swearing indicates corruption of the cognitive faculty, and from this arises the loss of reverence for truth. Its possessor therefore does not recognize what is good nor denounce what is evil, and so he swears whether truthfully or falsely, as it happens. ﴿Contemptible﴾, that is, despicable, weak, base in resolve and manliness, and base in judgment. This is because a person does not swear much unless he imagines within himself that he will not be believed except by swearing, since he has no dignity or majesty in the eyes of the one he speaks to that would cause him to be believed. He prefers idleness because it suits his nature, and that is the greatest baseness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 11:

Whenever someone is characterized by a quality, he loves that people share it with him or come close to him, especially if that quality is base, so that he is spared blame or being alone in it. And because a thing that is near to something else resembles it, He said: ﴿backbiter﴾, that is, one who frequently finds fault with people in their absence. Al-Hasan said: "He is the one who jabs at his brother in the gathering." That is because al-hamz (الهمز, pressing, squeezing, pushing) is biting, pressing, and pushing, and it derives from al-mihmaz (المِهْمَاز, the spur), which is used to prick the bellies of animals. It is specific to backbiting, just as al-lamz (اللمز, slander) is specific to confrontation.

Since al-namimah (النميمة, tale-bearing), which is conveying speech in the manner of stirring up mischief, is the most severe form of hamz, it indicates that he does this and does not confine himself to mere transmission, but rather carries it to others, even if they are distant. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿a constant walker about with slander﴾, that is, one who walks about a great deal, ﴿with slander﴾, that is, one who transmits what a person has said in confidence and spreads it secretly, while its owner does not want it revealed, in order to sow discord between people, striving to the utmost of his effort in doing so.

Since the one who is like this wants to elevate himself by belittling people, and since withholding is for the sake of monopolizing what is withheld, so that others are in need of him and devoted to him, (p-301) because it is in his nature that he binds himself only through greed and not through gratitude, the opposite of the generous person, who raises himself above greed and binds himself only through gratitude for favors, and so he is generous, supposing that people are like that; He said: ﴿withholding﴾, meaning, one who withholds greatly and intensely ﴿from the good﴾, meaning every good, whether of wealth, faith, or other things, from himself and from others, whether of religion or of this world, and so on.

Since the one who commits these disgraceful acts among people, and who limits his slander and backbiting to what has actually occurred, and in withholding to what is rightfully his to withhold, is miserly, [al-Biqa'i] made clear that he is not content with that, but rather goes beyond it by exerting effort in what makes him even baser. So He said: ﴿transgressor﴾, meaning, constantly overstepping the limits in all of that, ﴿sinful﴾, meaning, exceeding in committing what necessitates sin, so he abandons the good things, takes up the evil ones, desires sins and seeks them out, and forsakes acts of obedience and shuns them.

When everyone who has these base qualities, which tend to drive people away from him and make them shun him, strives to conceal them, if he is sensible, through gentleness, humility, deception and easy compliance (p-302), the verse states that this is otherwise. It alerts to this with the phrase of distance, saying: ﴿Coarse﴾, meaning: a great eater, extremely contentious, harsh and crude in his character. His character is heavy and bitter, as if he were a piece of a mountain cut off from the rest. He cannot be drawn toward goodness except with difficulty, hardship and violence. It is said: "ʿatala him" when one leads him harshly. He is at the furthest extreme of stubbornness of disposition and unwillingness to be pliant toward goodness and to be impressed by it.

Al-Razi said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the ʿutull (the coarse one), and he said: "He is the one who is severe in character, broad in belly, a great eater, a great drinker, and a wrongdoer." Glorified is He, alerting to his persistence in those shameful acts, which necessitates that he is absorbed in them throughout his time and states, by omitting the preposition, said: ﴿After all that﴾. This refers to the character worthy of being avoided at great effort, which combines these qualities that have reached the utmost ugliness, until they became as if they were one firm, established trait, with no remedy for treating it. This is alerted to by His saying: ﴿Of doubtful birth﴾, meaning that he has become marked with evil, with bad reputation and ugly praise, and that he is known by it, just as a sheep is known by its zanama (the dangling flesh under its throat), which hangs and sways. The servant is known by his faults and base character. It is also said: the zanim is the one who imitates a people while not being of them at all. The use of this term is not without an indication that he is a pretender (daʿiyy) whose lineage is not established with those to whom he claims to belong, so that he is cut off from all goodness, even if he is ascribed to noble fathers. It is taken from the zanama of a camel, which is a piece of skin cut from its ear and left hanging, and this is done only to noble camels.

All these actions are contrary to the courage that requires its possessor to be kind to everyone, to take no one into account, and not to let harm reach anyone except after his evil has become evident. Then he is treated according to justice, in a way that does not disgrace manliness. The one referred to by this, while the reference is general, is said to be al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It is said to be al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. It is said to be al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth. Ibn Qutayba said: We do not know that Allah the Exalted described anyone or mentioned his faults as He mentioned the faults of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

Since all the trash of this world is a passing, transient possession and a shrinking, vanishing shadow, one should not take pride in it, nor even pay attention to it, except one who has these attributes. So when his greatest concern and the extent of his knowledge is this, it produces in him haughtiness toward rights and arrogance toward the servants, [Allah] said: ﴿That﴾, meaning, because ﴿he was possessed of wealth﴾, meaning one mentioned for abundance of it, ﴿and sons﴾. We had bestowed favor upon him with them, so he came to be obeyed on their account, (p-304) and so he was in a state where he ought to have thanked Us for them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 68, verse 15:

﴿When Our verses are recited﴾, i.e., are mentioned in the manner of following, ﴿to him﴾, even if that was specifically for him, ﴿Our verses﴾, i.e., the signs that indicate, with the utmost clarity, the Supreme King and the attributes of greatness that belong to Him. ﴿He says﴾, i.e., he rushed to utter this statement without reflection or pause, instead of [ʿiwaḍan -] gratitude. The phrase ʾinna ("that") with its preposition (jārihi) is connected to what the speech implies, like *kadhaba* ("he lied") for the reason of his being established [in wealth]. It is not connected to *qāla* ("he says"), because that is the apodosis of the condition (jawāb al-sharṭ). It is also permissible for it to be connected to ﴿do not obey﴾, meaning: his obedience is not to be found for a reason, if he is such-and-such. It was also read with a kasra (*in*, "if"), on the basis that it is conditional (*sharṭiyya*), so the prohibition of obeying him for the cause of wealth implies the prohibition of obeying him when described by other than it, by way of a fortiori reasoning, like the causing of infanticide by poverty. ﴿Tales﴾ is the plural of *sutūr*, which is the plural of *saṭr* (line). ﴿Of the ancients﴾, i.e., things they wrote down and recorded, and finished with. His base nature led him to pride himself on his wealth, so it drew him into denying what is the greatest thing one can hear. He made disbelief the place of gratitude, and he was not ashamed of the fact that everyone who hears him knows his lie. So he turned away from gratitude and put disbelief in its place. This is evidence for all those previous attributes, with the reasoning being attributed to what is, to the rational person, more delusive and weaker than the spider's house (p. 305). Relying on it alone is sufficient for being characterized by firm established baseness. The phrase ʾan qāla ("that he said") is not governed by ... rather by what the context implies, because what falls within the scope of the condition does not govern what comes before it.

When this man had sunk deep into evil, the listener anticipated his recompense. So He said, informing that He would bring upon him such disgrace and exposure that he would become notorious among creation in this world and the Hereafter: ﴿We will brand him﴾, meaning We will make the shame that befalls him in both abodes like a branding mark whose trace will never fade. The Arabs say: "He branded him with a bad brand" (wasamahu misama su'in).

Since the branding mark is a wound, and placing it in a spot that cannot be concealed makes it more painful, and since the face is the noblest part of a human being, and the most prominent and honored part of it is the nose, which is why they made it the seat of honor and zeal and derived from it the word al-anafah (pride/disdain), He said: ﴿upon the snout﴾, meaning upon the long nose entirely and what borders it of the two cheeks, a mark elevated over it with great clarity, so that it would be a public humiliation among people, a disgrace to his people, and a degradation and shame. Indeed, for my life, this was so for him, through this shameful mention and the vile sin of disbelief and what accompanies it. And there will be for him on the Great Day of Gathering something even more shameful than this. Moreover, this branding was actualized in the world physically, in that his nose was struck on the Day of Badr with a blow (p-306) that crushed it. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The expression of the nose by this term is for belittling and disdain.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 17:

When [He] mentioned at the beginning of the sovereignty [in the surah] that He created death and life to test [people] through their deeds, and concluded here with the reproach of the one who is deceived by wealth and children while knowing that death lies ahead of him, He repeated the mention of the test and emphasized it, because their deeds, together with their knowledge that it is a passing accident, [belong to] those who think that sovereignty is lasting and that their disposal of affairs is complete. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them﴾, meaning: We dealt with them, according to the greatness that is ours, those whom We brand on the snouts from Quraysh and the rest of Our servants, with what We extended to them, dealing with them as one who tests while We know the outward and the inward. So that [favor] deceived them, and they supposed that they were beloved, while those whom We restricted from among Our friends were enemies. So they despised them and, because of their scarcity in worldly matters, attributed to them folly, madness, error and corruption. Thus it is near that We will seize them suddenly, as We did with the people of the garden. Therefore, everyone who saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was tested by him: if he believed, he was among those who did good deeds, and otherwise he was among those who did evil.

(p-307) When the common people of Mecca did not recognize Allah's blessing upon them through him (ﷺ), Allah removed him from among them and honored him with helpers, making him the greatest of honors for them. Everyone who heard of him and did not believe is in the same situation: his deeds are like this garden, which he thinks is something, but it betrays him at the time he most needs it. Or [the meaning is that] Our testing of them was through the famine for which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, until they ate carrion, yet they did not repent as [others] repented. ﴿As We tested﴾, that is, tested, by dealing with them as one who tests while We know the outward and the inward. Its outcome is that He brings out what is in the inner selves, so that the servants may know it in the world of witnessing just as the Creator knows it in the unseen world. Or it is a metaphor for the requital. ﴿The people of the garden﴾: He identified them because it was well known among them. It was a great orchard two farsakhs (parasangs) from Sana'a, called al-Dhirwan, which travelers passed through. Its owner used to call out to the poor at the time of harvest (al-siram, cutting of the crop) and leave for them what the sickle missed, or what the wind blew down, or what fell beyond the mat spread under the palm tree. When he died, his sons were stingy with this, so they swore to cut it before dawn, so that the poor would not come except after they had finished. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿they swore﴾, and [the Qur'an] indicated the emphasis of the oath, so He said: ﴿they would surely cut it off﴾. He expressed by it the harvesting, because it indicates a decisive, resolved cutting, complete and uprooting, preventing the poor, so that it would be a cutting from every aspect. It is derived from al-sarim, a stick placed across the mouth of a kid so that it does not suckle, and from al-sarma', a desert with no water in it, and a she-camel with little milk. ﴿Early in the morning﴾ [al-Qalam: 21], that is, entering at the first part of the morning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 18:

﴿Wa-lā﴾ — that is, while the situation is that they [do] not ﴿yastathnūna﴾ — that is, they do not seek, nor do they bring about, any exception (thunya, meaning a turning back) to what preceded the oath, by saying "in shā' Allāh" (if God wills) or by any other of the words that would make it so that some part of their garden would be unrestricted and not prevented. This is called istithnā' (exception, in the sense of a carve-out) because it is the removal of something whose ruling is other than what was mentioned first. The original form of it was: "illā an yashā'a Allāh" (except if God wills), and "in shā' Allāh" (if God wills) is attached to it because it returns to it in the unity of the ruling.

﴿Then there swept over it﴾: i.e., as a consequence of their deeds, this ambitious one (the one who aspired to more), a punishment swept over ﴿it﴾, that is, their garden, ﴿a visitation﴾ (ṭā'if), i.e., a destroying, all-encompassing punishment. Although this is a very easy matter with God, it is great relative to the garden, because it left nothing of it. A visitation (ṭā'if) in this sense occurs only at night, so it is said, but this is refuted by the verse:

﴿When a visitation from Satan touches them, they remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 201].

Since this was outwardly a punishment, he informed that in meaning it was kindness and training, by saying ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One known for a greatness without limit and for His kindness to you. He is therefore worthy of disciplining your people so that they accept from you, as He disciplined the companions of the garden with what obliged their repentance. He is the one worthy of training the servants, so that they understand you and become fit to abstain from the world and to turn to lofty matters. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., while the state was that the companions of the garden, who swore (to harvest it in secret), ﴿were sleeping﴾ at the time the visitation was sent (p. 309).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 20:

﴿So it became﴾ [i.e.] as a consequence of this circuit (ṭā'if) sent by the All-Powerful, who neither becomes heedless nor sleeps, upon the fate of those who are still captives of incapacity [and sleep], in deed or in potential, that their garden became, at the time they were to harvest it in the morning and rejoice in it, ﴿like the dark-cut [garden]﴾ — i.e., like trees whose fruit has been cut off, or like a thing between which and its goal the connection has been severed, so that there is no reaching it in any way. It was also said: like the pitch-black night; and it was said: like black ash, with no fruit in it, because that circuit (ṭā'if) had destroyed it and left nothing in it, since they sought all of it and did not give its due (zakāh) by that which would ward off the calamities from it — the opposite of what their father had: the fruit of his righteous deed, which was protection of his wealth and blessing in all his affairs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 21:

When they, owing to the strength of their resolve upon what they had sworn, were as though they had an appointment, there followed from this his saying: ﴿So they called out to one another⁠﴾, that is, it was as though each of them was calling to the other ﴿at daybreak⁠﴾, that is, at the very beginning of their entering upon the morning. He explained the calling out by his saying:

"Go early to your tilth" — that is, be up early in the morning, coming and taking possession and being able to reach your tilth (ḥarth), i.e., the place of your profit which you have improved and toiled over, so that no one other than yourselves deserves it. It seems they delayed their rising and going out, so they [their companion] restrained them by his saying (p-310): ﴿If you are going to harvest﴾, that is, today, as a state that belongs to you with the utmost desire, ﴿resolute﴾, that is, cutting the fruit (judhdh) so that it is wholly yours with no one else sharing with you, as you agreed among yourselves; or [it means] determined in what you resolved upon. He expressed their haste to go with his saying:

So they set off, by reason of this urging and right after it, as though they had been prepared. ﴿And they﴾ — that is, while the state they were in was that they ﴿were speaking in low tones﴾ — that is, they were saying, as they went, words that were in the utmost secrecy, as though they were going off to steal from a house that was under the strictest guard. The word (yatakhafatun) comes from al-khufut, which means quietness and stillness. Then he explained what they were saying in low tones with His words:

﴿That no needy person shall enter it today against you.﴾ They emphasized this because they could not believe that anyone would reach such shamelessness and hardness of face, or that Judhadh would be empty of a beggar.

Since custom dictates that a person is bound to forget something, or to leave a door or a gap open, through which a poor man may enter, and because of it, they said: ﴿today﴾, meaning throughout the whole day. This is indicated by the omission of the preposition (nazʿ al-khāfiḍ, the dropping of the governing particle). They meant that they would go round repeatedly and search, so that they would leave no fruit and no spot where anyone might hope, by coming to them, to gain anything. ﴿Against you﴾, meaning while you are in it, ﴿a needy man﴾. The phrase "no needy person shall enter" is in the form of a prohibition addressed to the needy man, in order to intensify the prohibition they placed upon themselves, that they would not let him enter upon them. Their most moderate in age, best in disposition and most just in nature then said to them, as indicated by what follows: "Do not say this, and do from goodness what your father used to do." It seems that God, exalted is He, left out (ṭawā) his reply, because although it is indicated by what follows, he did not give preference to anything. He emphasized that their setting out at the time of morning was by his saying:

"And they set out early in the morning" — that is, they went to it at dawn, ﴿and they set out early in the morning﴾ — "with determined purpose" (ḥard), which is not otherwise, and it means intent (al-qaṣd), intense anger, firm resolve about the matter, obstinacy in it, haste, and gloom at withholding and scarcity of good, from ḥāradat al-sanah, meaning there was no rain in the year, and al-ibil, meaning the camels withheld their milk; and ḥard means when one hastens. ﴿Confident⁠﻿﻿ of their ability﴾ in their own estimation and in their assumption, as evidenced by their not making the exception (istithnā'), for firm resolve to act in the future, let alone with a break of the oath, is the act of one who has no equal.

Note: the Arabic text has been transliterated and glossed as requested; the quoted verse is rendered as "and they set out early in the morning, with determined purpose, confident of their ability."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 26:

﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْها﴾ That is, after a short journey, and there was no trace of crop or fruit on it. ﴿قالُوا﴾ Because, due to the bad state it had come to from that calamity, it had become far from the condition it was in when they were apart and their intentions had changed; so its appearance bewildered them and its state astounded them. They emphasized (their words), because their being lost (on the way) would not be believed given how recent their acquaintance with it was, how much they had frequented it, and how strong their knowledge of it was. So they said: ﴿إنّا لَضالُّونَ﴾ That is, we have strayed from the way to our garden, because this (garden) does not resemble it in any respect, in terms of the freshness, heavy yield, and fine appearance it had yesterday.

When the thing that had stunned them became clear, [immediately] they said, turning away from their error: ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ That is: our deprivation of the good that was in it is established, the good from which we were absent only during the darkness of the night. So God deprived us of it because of what we resolved upon, the depriving of the needy, (p-312) for God does not change what is with a people until they change what is with themselves.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 28:

When afflicting calamities are, by their nature, a likely cause of softening of the heart and of repentance for one for whom good is intended, and of increased disbelief for another, [Allah] resumed with His statement: ﴿The most upright of them in opinion, intellect, age, leadership and virtue said﴾ [i.e., in opinion] and intellect and age and leadership and virtue, disapproving of them: ﴿Did I not tell you?﴾ that what you have done is not becoming, and that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is on watch (bi-l-mirsad) over whoever alters what is in himself and deviates.

When the withholding of good, especially in [a case] like this one, implies an assumption of deficiency in Allah, the Exalted, either that He, glorified is He, does not fail to fulfill what was pledged in charity, or that He is not able to destroy what the human being was stingy with, [the speaker] said, resuming: ﴿Why not?﴾ That is, why did you not, and why do you not, ﴿glorify [Allah]﴾ — that is, render declaration of His transcendence, glorified and exalted is He, above what your action has suggested. The least of glorification is the exception clause (al-istithna') when taking an oath, expressing doubt about human ability and affirming the power of the King, the Judge, while calling to mind His greatness, glorified and exalted is He. The context of the discourse indicates that they were prepared for repentance, by His saying:

﴿قالُوا﴾ without hesitation, regarding what had befallen them from their father's blessing. Then He (glorified is He), relating their words, said: ﴿سُبْحانَ رَبِّنا﴾, meaning: the One who does good to us is exalted above the greatest exaltation, far above having committed any wrong in what He did to us. They emphasized the ugliness of their deed, abasing themselves and submitting to their Lord, [ و-] affirming their repentance, because the state they had been in required that their turning back from it not be believed. [They said] ﴿إنّا كُنّا﴾, meaning: by what was in our natures of corruption, ﴿ظالِمِينَ﴾, meaning: firmly fixed in placing things in other than their proper places, since we did not resolve firmly upon what our father used to do of righteousness. [ ثُمَّ حَيَّتْ حَلِفُنا عَلى تَرْكِ ذَلِكَ ثُمَّ حَيْثُ لَمْ نَرُدَّ الأمْرَ إلى اللَّهِ بِالِاسْتِثْناءِ حَيْثُ حَلَفْنا - ] for the exception ( istithna') is a declaration of God's transcendence above anything occurring in His dominion that He does not will. Then He affirmed their repentance with His words, which are a consequence of their acknowledgment of wrongdoing:

Then some of them turned toward others (ʾaqbala baʿḍuhum), in the very act of hastening to submission (ʾay fī ḥāli mubādaratihim ilā al-khuḍūʿ), "toward others" (ʿalā baʿḍin); and the parallelism (al-taswiya) between their two groups in the wording indicates equality in repentance (al-tawba). "They blame one another" (yatalāwamūn) means that each of them does toward the other, in blaming them, for what he intended of withholding and for abandoning what they had abandoned of giving and repelling, the same as what the other does toward him; and the deficiency is attributed to him, as is the custom of the defeated and the powerless.

"Then, when the listener was eager to know [some of] that, He said: ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were transgressors."﴾" — no, let me translate precisely.

The listener, once eager to learn about that, is answered: ﴿They said﴾, calling out, because their nearness to him and his constant presence occupied them from everything else: ﴿"Woe to us!"﴾ — that is, "This is the time of your presence, O Woe, upon us, and of your calling to us, for we have no companion except you." Woe (al-Waylu) is ruin and being on the verge of it.

When the base people denied that one who withholds from the poor could be a transgressor, they emphasized their statement: ﴿"Indeed we were"﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿transgressors﴾, that is, exceeding the bounds in what we did by agreeing together to withhold from the poor and to cut the harvest in the morning without making the exception of "If God wills." It would have been possible, if we had to do it at all, to do so without an oath, without concealment from others, and without speaking in a whisper while walking, by saying to the poor: "God will open [for you]" and similar words.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 32:

When they put forward what is more beneficial for them than the mutual blame, which necessarily leads to their unanimous agreement on repentance, and thereby the regret that is the sign of repentance became known, they resumed (with a statement) as an answer to one who asks: Did they confine themselves to mutual blame? Their saying: ﴿Perhaps﴾, meaning it is possible [that it will be], and it is worthy and fitting that it will be: ﴿our Lord﴾, meaning the One who showed kindness to us by raising this garden and now by destroying its fruit as a discipline for us, ﴿will give us in exchange﴾, meaning in place of our garden, ﴿something better than it﴾, that will set right for us the affair of our livelihood, so that our present states, in which we are in worry and shabbiness, will turn into joy and delight, by what the placing of the verb upon their pronoun conveys. The reading of Abu 'Amr and Nafi' is with the doubled consonant (yubaddilana, with tashdid), and the reading of the rest is with the single consonant (yubdilana, with takhfif), and both are close in meaning, except that the doubled form indicates gradualness, so the single form is more eloquent in meaning. Our hope is attached only to the cause of our repentance and to our knowledge that our Lord is capable of what He wills, and none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.

When this supplication indicated their turning to Allah alone, they stated it explicitly and emphasized it, because their former state was that of one who denies such (turning) from himself. So they said, giving the reason: ﴿Indeed, we﴾. Since the situation calls for repentance and turning back from the sin, they expressed (the matter) with the particle of ending, as an indication of their distance from the divine presences, out of courtesy on their part, and they said: ﴿to our Lord﴾, meaning the One who showed kindness to us and nurtured us by bringing us into existence and then sustaining us, specifically, not to other than Him, glorified is He, ﴿are desirous﴾, meaning our desire and our hope for good and honour after pardon are firmly established. It has been said that Allah, exalted is His power, before their return, replaced it for them, giving them in exchange a garden called al-Hayawan, such that a single cluster of it would be carried by one man alone because of the abundance of its herbage. This is related by al-Baghawi from Ibn Mas'ud. But since the situation calls for warning against one who relies on his wealth and despises the weak among the servants of Allah, and does not honour them with His majesty, He concealed (this), and mentioned what shaped this speech and produced it, namely the equating of the state of Quraysh and the state of these (people) in bounty and prolonged forbearance, together with their contempt for His friends and their presumption against them through His favours and blessings. So He said, warning:

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this affliction with which We tested the people of the Garden, [the destruction of what they had], while they were in the utmost confidence in their power over it and their certainty of it, along with their approval of their own deed and their conviction that it was right. The people of Makkah were threatened with the same, yet they did not hasten to repent. ﴿The punishment﴾ with which you warn them [of it -] and frighten them with in this world (dunya, the worldly life). When the term We had decreed for it is fulfilled, We seize them with it, neither hastening nor delaying, for only one who is deficient and fears missing out hastens.

Since they denied the matters of the Hereafter (akhira) more strongly than they denied the matters of this world, He emphasized His statement: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾, that is, the punishment that will occur there for the disobedient and the tyrants, ﴿greater﴾, that is, greater than anything they imagine.

Since this is something that should move anyone with the slightest awareness to flee from it, He said: ﴿if only they knew﴾, that is, if the disbelievers had any knowledge of anything of their own natural dispositions at any time, they would have turned back from what they are engaged in, which they know displeases God, and so it would be the cause of punishment in both abodes. Yet, despite this, they are stricken in the sight of God and in the sight of people by those vile effects, among them false oaths, which indicate [their lack of -] courage and the feebleness of their intellects. But they have no kind of knowledge now, and one who is sealed by dying in disbelief will not have any kind of knowledge renewed for him, whereas another will return at the time God has decreed for him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 68, verse 34:

(p-317) When he had mentioned the fate of the people of rigidity (jumud), who do not allow for the possible (al-mumakkanat) (ﷺ? no; the term refers to contingent possibilities), he mentioned their opposites, saying, emphatically in order to refute their denial: ﴿Indeed, for the God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾, meaning the deeply rooted in the attribute of taqwa (God-consciousness), specifically and not others who are not God-conscious. Taqwa is guarding oneself by a shield, motivated by fear of what harms, and what motivates it is allowing for the possible (tajwiz al-mumakkanat). Al-Mulawi said: Its origin is that the wary horse, which is the one with a sore, unshod hoof, does not place its hoof until it sees whether the place is soft and suitable. Likewise the God-conscious person does not move or rest except upon insight (basirah) from the pleasure of God in that.
